person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: Here we present a principled statistical framework for discerning and quantifying power-law behavior in empirical data.

span.label: power-law distributions in empirical data
span.quote: Power-law distributions occur in many situations of scientific interest and have significant consequences for our understanding of natural and man-made phenomena.

span.label: simulation
span.quote: We evaluate the effectiveness of the approach with tests on synthetic data and give critical comparisons to previous approaches.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the lower bound of the power-law range is chosen by minimising the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the empirical distribution and the best-fit model above that bound - too high a bound shrinks the data and too low a one includes non-power-law points, so the minimum lies between
span.quote: The fundamental idea behind this method is simple: we choose the value of ˆxmin that makes the probability distributions of the measured data and the best-fit power-law model as similar as possible above ˆxmin. In general, if we choose ˆxmin higher than the true value xmin, then we are effectively reducing the size of our data set, which will make the probability distributions a poorer match because of statistical fluctuation. Conversely, if we choose ˆxmin smaller than the true xmin, the distributions will differ because of the fundamental difference between the data and model by which we are describing it. In between lies our best estimate.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: each synthetic data set is scored against ITS OWN best-fit power law rather than against the distribution it was drawn from, which is what makes the resulting p-value unbiased: the synthetic sets undergo exactly the calculation the real data underwent, fitting included
span.quote: Note crucially that for each synthetic data set we compute the KS statistic relative to the best-fit power law for that data set, not relative to the original distribution from which the data set was drawn. In this way we ensure that we are performing for each synthetic data set the same calculation that we performed for the real data set, a crucial requirement if we wish to get an unbiased estimate of the p-value.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: synthetic data are generated semiparametrically - drawn from the fitted power law with probability equal to the observed tail fraction, and otherwise resampled from the observed points below the cut-off - so the synthetic sets share the empirical body while following the power law in the tail
span.quote: To obtain accurate estimates of p we need synthetic data that have a distribution similar to the empirical data below xmin but that follow the fitted power law above xmin. To generate such data we make use of a semiparametric approach. Suppose that our observed data set has ntail observations x xmin and n observations in total. We generate a new data set with n observations as follows. With probability ntail/n we generate a random number xi drawn from a power law with scaling parameter ˆα and x xmin. Otherwise, with probability 1 ntail/n, we select one element uniformly at random from among the elements of the observed data set that have x < xmin and set xi equal to that element. Repeating the process for all i = 1 . . . n we generate a complete synthetic data set that indeed follows a power law above xmin but has the same (non-power-law) distribution as the observed data below.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the test distribution is constructed to be hard rather than convenient: it is exponential below the cut-off and a power law above, and its slope is CONTINUOUS at the cut-off, so it deviates only gently from the power law below that point - the authors' word is challenging
span.quote: This distribution follows a power law at xmin and above but an exponential below. Furthermore, it has a continuous slope at xmin and thus deviates only gently from the power law as we pass below this point, making for a challenging test.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: uncertainty on the fitted parameters is obtained by a nonparametric bootstrap - drawing a fresh sequence of n points uniformly at random from the original data and re-estimating both the lower bound and the scaling parameter on each surrogate set
span.quote: One way to do this is to make use of a nonparametric “bootstrap” method [16]. Given our n measurements, we generate a synthetic data set with a similar distribution to the original by drawing a new sequence of points xi, i = 1 . . . n uniformly at random from the original data. Using either method described above, we then estimate xmin and α for this surrogate data set.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the alternative goodness-of-fit statistics are tested rather than assumed: reweighted KS and Kuiper behave like plain KS, while Anderson-Darling returns cut-offs an order of magnitude too large, and the cost of that conservatism is stated as fewer tail observations, larger error on the scaling parameter and less ability to validate the model
span.quote: We have performed tests with each of these alternative statistics and find that results for the reweighted KS and Kuiper statistics are very similar to those for the standard KS statistic. The Anderson-Darling statistic, on the other hand, we find to be highly conservative in this application, giving estimates ˆxmin that are too large by an order of magnitude or more. When there are many samples in the tail of the distribution this degree of conservatism may be acceptable, but in most cases the reduction in the number of tail observations greatly increases the statistical error on our MLE for the scaling parameter and also reduces our ability to validate the power-law model.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the number of synthetic data sets is fixed by the precision wanted in the p-value rather than by convention, derived from the test's expected worst-case performance
span.quote: We also need to decide how many synthetic data sets to generate. Based on an analysis of the expected worst-case performance of the test, a good rule of thumb turns out to be the following: if we wish our p-values to be accurate to within about

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the direction of the p-value is inverted relative to its ordinary use: the quantity being tested is the model the authors want to assess rather than a null, so a HIGH p-value is the favourable one and a low value rules the power law out
span.quote: Here, by contrast, we use the p-value as a measure of the hypothesis we are trying to verify, and hence high values, not low, are “good.”

span.label: one can never confirm a power law, only find data consistent with it
span.quote: The most we can say is that our observations are consistent with the hypothesis

span.label: few empirical phenomena obey power laws across the whole range of x
span.quote: few empirical phenomena obey power laws for all values of x

span.label: Known sampling biases in several of the reanalysed data sets were left uncorrected.
span.quote: We have not attempted to correct any biases in our analysis.

span.label: Many of the reanalysed data sets are partial samples of larger populations.
span.quote: Many of these data sets are only subsets of much larger entities (such as the web sites, which are only a small fraction of the entire web).

span.label: The framework is presented only for the power law; no extension to other distributional forms is given.
span.quote: In principle, they could also be extended to other, non-power-law distributions as well, although we have not given such an extension here.

span.label: The procedure often cannot separate power-law from log-normal behaviour.
span.quote: In general, we find that it is extremely difficult to tell the difference between log-normal and power-law behavior.

span.label: Two model forms indistinguishable on the observed data can give enormously different extrapolations into the tail, which is where such fits are usually applied.
span.quote: if we wish to extrapolate a fitted distribution far into its tail, to predict, for example, the frequencies of large but rare events like major earthquakes or meteor impacts, then conclusions based on different fitted forms can differ enormously even if the forms are indistinguishable in the domain covered by the actual data.

span.label: Seven of the twenty-four data sets previously conjectured to be power laws are firmly ruled out.
span.quote: The p-values in Table 6.1 indicate that 17 of the 24 data sets are consistent with a power-law distribution. The remaining seven data sets all have p-values small enough that the power-law model can be firmly ruled out.

span.label: Two published scaling parameters for the same citation data disagree with each other and with this paper's maximum-likelihood estimate.
span.quote: the citation distribution data of [48] have been reported to have a scaling parameter of either 2.9 [62] or 2.5 [33], neither of which are compatible with our maximum likelihood figure of 3.16

span.label: The accept/reject verdict rests on a stated p-value threshold of 0.1.
span.quote: If the resulting p-value is greater than 0.1 the power law is a plausible hypothesis for the data, otherwise it is rejected.

span.label: The range fitted is chosen, and that choice controls how much data the test sees.
span.quote: since we fit the power-law form to only the part of the distribution above xmin, the value of xmin effectively controls how many data points we have to work with.

span.label: Errors run in both directions on small samples: a power law can look like a good fit to non-power-law data, and true power laws cannot be separated from alternatives.
span.quote: it is difficult to rule out alternative fits to such data, even when they are truly power-law distributed, and conversely the power-law form may appear to be a good fit even when the data are drawn from a non-power-law distribution.
